title: Vagus Signal Router
description: Interactive model of two-way traffic on the vagus nerve. Learners trigger a meal, fat arriving (CCK), gut inflammation, or a stressful thought and watch afferent signals travel up to the nucleus tractus solitarius and efferent signals travel down from the dorsal motor nucleus. A separate spinal route shows that the vagus is not the only gut-brain wire, and a vagotomy switch shows what happens when the vagus is cut.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Compare afferent (gut-to-brain) and efferent (brain-to-gut) signaling along the vagus nerve for a meal, fat arriving, gut inflammation, and a stressful thought.
Explain why most vagus nerve traffic is sensory, using the 8-of-10 fiber bundle based on classic animal fiber counts.
Contrast the vagal route with the spinal route and predict which signals still reach the brain after vagotomy.
prerequisites: The autonomic nervous system and its role in digestion
The enteric nervous system as the gut's local nerve network
Basic idea of a neuron carrying signals in one direction
keyQuestions: Which direction does most vagus nerve traffic travel?
How does the brainstem turn a stretch signal into a command that relaxes the stomach?
Which gut signals travel by spinal nerves instead of the vagus?
What still works, and what stops, after the vagus nerve is cut?
misconceptions: The vagus nerve mostly sends commands from the brain to the gut.
The vagus nerve is the only route between the gut and the brain.
The vagus nerve is just a 'calm down' switch.
Cutting the vagus nerve stops all gut sensations.
